answer_text:
Climate change has wide-ranging and deeply damaging effects on ocean life. Here is a comprehensive overview:

---

## 🌊 Effects of Climate Change on Ocean Life

### 1. 🌡️ Rising Ocean Temperatures & Marine Heatwaves
Life in most of the global ocean, from pole to pole and from sea surface to the abyssal depths, is already experiencing higher temperatures due to human-driven climate change. Warmer sea temperatures disturb the sensitive balance within ocean habitats and affect where and how sea creatures live and act.

Marine heatwaves take a major toll on marine life — for example, due to fallout from the 2019–2021 Pacific Northwest marine heatwave, Bering Sea snow crab populations declined 84% between 2018 and 2022, a loss of 9.8 billion crabs. Scientists predict that the frequency, duration, scale, and intensity of marine heatwaves will increase, as sea surface temperatures continue to rise with global warming.

---

### 2. 🪸 Coral Reef Destruction
Dubbed the "rainforests of the sea," coral reefs are home to more than 25% of marine life in the world, including more than 4,000 fish species, as well as turtles, plants, invertebrates, and marine mammals. Warming ocean temperatures can lead to coral bleaching — the sudden die-off of large parts of coral reefs. The UN Environment Programme says that every one of the world's coral reefs could bleach by the end of the century if the water continues to warm. Coral bleaching occurs as reefs lose their life-sustaining microscopic algae when under stress.

A warming of 1.5°C threatens to destroy 70 to 90 percent of coral reefs, and a 2°C increase means a nearly 100 percent loss — a point of no return.

---

### 3. 🧪 Ocean Acidification
Increased carbon dioxide in the air makes oceans acidic. It occurs when seawater absorbs carbon dioxide and mixes it with water to form carbonic acid, decreasing ocean pH. The acid in the water can badly affect sea creatures that need calcium carbonate to make their shells and bones. These creatures act as carbon stores, which helps mitigate climate change, but as their shells dissolve, this natural way of removing carbon from the atmosphere is threatened.

---

### 4. 💨 Ocean Deoxygenation
Overall ocean oxygen concentrations are estimated to have declined 2% over 50 years from the 1960s. Low oxygen represents a stress for almost all marine animals. Very low oxygen levels create regions with much reduced fauna, and it is predicted that these low oxygen zones will expand in the future due to climate change, representing a serious threat to marine life.

---

### 5. 🐟 Shifts in Species Distribution & Biodiversity Loss
Widespread changes have been observed, including damage to coral reefs and mangroves that support ocean life, and migration of species to higher latitudes and altitudes where the water could be cooler. Latest estimates from UNESCO warn that more than half of the world's marine species may stand on the brink of extinction by 2100.

---

### 6. 🌱 Decline of Phytoplankton
One of the most critical changes brought about by global warming is the ongoing reduction of phytoplankton. These tiny plants are an integral food source for ocean life and are responsible for around half of the world's photosynthetic activity. Essentially, they are the foundations of the oceanic food chain, so a reduction in their numbers creates a knock-on effect that ripples up the entire food chain.

---

### 7. ⚠️ The "Deadly Trio"
Scientists refer to increased global warming, ocean acidification, and increased deoxygenation as climate change's "deadly trio." When these occur at the same time, the synergistic effects damage marine life and ecosystem structure and functions. The deadly trio leads to biodiversity loss and degraded ecosystem functions and structures. In parallel, ecosystem services suffer — for instance, there are reduced catches of commercially important fisheries, and blue carbon ecosystems have less capacity to store carbon.

---

### The Bigger Picture
A study published in 2025 projected that rising ocean temperatures, together with other climate-driven stressors, will more than double cumulative impacts on marine ecosystems by mid-century. At a 1.1°C increase in temperature today, an estimated 60 percent of the world's marine ecosystems have already been degraded or are being used unsustainably.

The health of the ocean is deeply intertwined with the health of the entire planet, making addressing climate change an urgent global priority.
